name: Additive bias
statement: Asked to improve something, people search first for things to add and seldom consider what could be taken away, even when removal is cheaper and works better.
meaning: The claim is about search rather than taste. Adams, Converse, Hales and Klotz do not argue that people prefer clutter, or that they reject subtractive ideas once those ideas are on the table. They argue that subtractive ideas arrive late in the mental list of candidate changes, or never arrive at all, so a satisfactory additive answer is accepted before the better subtractive one is generated. That predicts three specific things. Cueing subtraction should raise the rate of subtractive answers, repeated attempts at the same problem should raise it, and cognitive load should lower it. The Nature abstract states all three as findings. It also makes the bias a property of the moment of searching, which is why prompts change the result and why nothing in the account requires anyone to dislike less.

origin.who: Gabrielle S. Adams, Benjamin A. Converse, Andrew H. Hales and Leidy E. Klotz
origin.note: Their paper is titled "People systematically overlook subtractive changes" and reports eight experiments. The name "additive bias" is not the paper's own label, which is the overlooking of subtractive changes.

evidence: The Nature paper is paywalled and this entry could not read past its abstract, so what follows separates the abstract from descriptions given by later papers. The abstract states the finding as three contrasts: participants were less likely to identify advantageous subtractive changes when the task did not cue them to consider subtraction, when they had only one opportunity rather than several to see the shortcomings of an additive search, and when they were under higher cognitive load. Meyvis and Yoon, writing the News and Views piece that ran alongside it, describe the first task. A Lego roof rests on a single corner pillar with a figurine underneath, each added block costs ten cents, and the cheap answer is to remove the pillar and let the roof sit on the base. Most participants added pillars instead. Fischer and colleagues describe the grid task from the later experiments: four ten-by-ten grids of white and green squares, made symmetrical by toggling squares either way. Fillon, Girandola, Bonnardel and Souchet, who replicated experiments 2 to 4, describe those as online tasks in which participants listed ideas to improve a drawing of a golf hole or to make it worse. In their summary table, the original's rate of participants producing at least one subtractive idea rose from 28 percent to 43 percent with a cue in experiments 2 and 3, from 21 percent to 48 percent in the improve condition of experiment 4, and from 28 percent to 50 percent in the make-worse condition. Those three pairs are quoted from Fillon and colleagues rather than read off the Nature paper.

replication.headline: The idea-generation experiments replicated in a large preregistered French sample; the Lego and grid tasks did not, once the instructions were counterbalanced.
replication.detail: Fillon and colleagues ran a preregistered replication of experiments 2 to 4 on 477 French adults recruited through Prolific, with 117 to 120 per condition. The asymmetry held: participants produced 1,155 additive ideas against 297 subtractive ones. The cue worked as in the original, raising the odds of listing at least one subtractive idea, OR = 2.52, 95% CI 1.73 to 3.71, p < .001. Broken out, the share producing at least one subtractive idea went from 26.5 percent to 43.8 percent in the improve condition and from 46.2 percent to 70.1 percent in the make-worse condition. These figures were read off the authors' preprint, because the Journal of Creative Behavior version is paywalled. Juvrud, Myers and Nyström went after the other two tasks and got a different answer. Testing 58 adults in Sweden and the United States and 58 Swedish children aged nine and ten, they counterbalanced the phrase "add or take away" against "take away or add" and rotated the orientation of the Lego tower. On the grid symmetry task, adults on the neutral patterns showed no difference between adding and subtracting, t(52) = -0.453, p = 0.653. On the Lego task they report no bias towards subtraction neglect across all participants, and the order of the two verbs in the instructions changed nothing. Their conclusion is that the effect depends on task, culture and age: Swedish adults subtracted more than American adults, and the children were more additive than the adults on the grid.

study.cite: Fillon, A. A., Girandola, F., Bonnardel, N., & Souchet, L. (2025). The overlooking of subtractive changes: Replication and extension to stronger cues and social norms. The Journal of Creative Behavior, 59(1), e1535.

limits: No replication of the whole set of eight experiments has been located. Fillon and colleagues took only experiments 2 to 4, the golf-hole idea listings, and chose them partly because they were the most social of the set. Juvrud and colleagues took the Lego and grid tasks, and their adult sample is 58 people split across two countries, which is small for a null result. Between them the two papers leave the cognitive-load manipulation and the repeated-attempt manipulation untested by anyone else this entry could find, searching Crossref, Nature's own citing-article lists and the Open Science Framework. Fischer, Winter, Felisatti, Myachykov, Mende and Shaki argue the original's materials tilt the result before any participant thinks. The instruction always ran "add or subtract" and never the reverse, a wording that matches ordinary usage: they report 95 occurrences of "add and subtract" and none of "subtract and add" in the Corpus of Contemporary American English. A latent semantic analysis put the supposedly neutral verbs "improve", "arrange" and "change" closer to addition, at 0.22, 0.33 and 0.22, than to subtraction, at 0.03, 0.14 and 0.16. They count the four grids as containing 73, 54, 68 and 56 white squares against 27, 46, 32 and 44 green ones, so 63 percent of the field was already white and the toggle was not symmetric in practice. Their point about toggling is the sharpest one: which direction counts as subtraction depends entirely on which colour is read as figure and which as ground. Fillon and colleagues also note that generality outside the West is untested, and report from the original's supplementary material that the subtractive transformation was produced by 77 percent of the American sample, 85 percent of the Japanese and 67 percent of the German. Those three figures come from their description, not from the source.
misreadings: The first error is reading the effect as a love of more. Nothing in the account says people value additions above subtractions; it says they think of additions first and stop searching. The cueing result is the test that separates the two, and it goes the way the search account predicts. The second error is treating the cue as a fix. In Fillon's replication the cue lifted the subtractive rate and the gap stayed wide, 1,155 additive ideas against 297, and their second experiment found a subtract-only cue beat the usual add-then-subtract wording. The third error is leaning on the Lego bridge. It is the image that carried the finding into the press, it is the origin story Klotz tells in his own account of the work, and it is the one task that has since failed to reproduce under counterbalanced instructions. Anyone quoting the Lego study as the proof is quoting the weakest part. The fourth error is filing this with omission bias or the status quo bias. Those are about preferring inaction or the current state; this is about which changes come to mind when action is already decided on, and a participant who bolts on three extra pillars has not been passive. The fifth error is treating the domain as settled. Barry and Adelina extended the question to mental health advice in 2025 and found additive advice recommended more often and rated more effective and feasible, which is a new domain rather than a re-run of the original tasks.
